description: AsteluneX Project  is a team dedicated to exploring the connection between Earth and the environments of Mars. Through our project we aim to develop an interactive platform that identifies and compares terrestrial locations with conditions analogous to potential permanent Martian bases. By combining planetary science, earth science, and interactive visualization, our goal is to make space exploration more accessible, engaging, and scientifically meaningful.
summary:
Mars Analog Explorer is an interactive scientific website developed to identify and investigate terrestrial environments in South America that share geological or environmental characteristics with Mars.

The project examines four potential analog sites: Yungay in Chile’s Atacama Desert, Salar de Antofalla in Argentina, Pali Aike Volcanic Field in Patagonia, and Laguna del Diamante in Argentina. Each location was analyzed using scientific literature, satellite observations from NASA Earthdata and Copernicus Sentinel-2, and geographic imagery.

The website features an interactive map, detailed scientific profiles, satellite visualizations, and an Earth–Mars comparison tool. These features allow users to explore similarities, differences, potential research applications, and limitations of each site.

By connecting Earth observation data with planetary science, Mars Analog Explorer addresses the challenge of identifying environments that could support research relevant to future Martian exploration. It highlights how terrestrial analogs can contribute to studying astrobiology, geological processes, robotic exploration, and environmental challenges.

Rather than claiming that these locations replicate Mars, the project emphasizes scientifically grounded comparisons, transparent uncertainty, and the importance of Earth-based research in preparing for future space missions.
details:
Project Details — Mars Analog Explorer

Mars Analog Explorer is an interactive scientific platform designed to investigate terrestrial environments that could serve as partial analogs for Martian exploration. The project combines planetary science, Earth observation data, geological research, and interactive web development to make scientific comparisons accessible and visually engaging.

How does it work?

The website features an interactive map of South America where users can select four terrestrial analog candidates: Yungay in Chile’s Atacama Desert, Salar de Antofalla in Argentina, Pali Aike Volcanic Field in Patagonia, and Laguna del Diamante in Argentina.

Each location has a detailed scientific profile covering its geography, environmental conditions, geology, mineralogy, satellite observations, scientific relevance, and limitations. An interactive Earth–Mars Comparison Lab allows users to explore similarities and differences between terrestrial environments and Martian geological processes.

The comparisons include Yungay’s relevance to astrobiology, Antofalla’s evaporitic similarities to Meridiani Planum, Pali Aike’s basaltic volcanic characteristics compared with Elysium Planitia, and Laguna del Diamante’s volcanic and periglacial features.

Tools and technologies

The research combined several scientific tools and datasets:

  • NASA Earthdata: Terra MODIS land surface temperature data (MOD11_L2), GPM IMERG precipitation estimates, and SRTM elevation data.
  • Copernicus Browser: Sentinel-2 Level-2A imagery, including True Color, SWIR, Moisture Index, and NDWI visualizations.
  • Google Earth: Geographic exploration, satellite imagery, and terrain observations.
  • Scientific literature: Geological, astrobiological, and planetary research, including information from SEGEMAR and CONAF.

The interactive website was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG, with AI-assisted web development through Claude and ChatGPT. The project was deployed using Netlify. Its interactive features include site selection, a schematic geographic map, scientific profiles, and comparative visualizations.

Creativity and innovation

The project’s main innovation is integrating different types of scientific evidence into a single interactive planetary exploration experience.

Rather than simply presenting a list of locations, Mars Analog Explorer allows users to investigate the scientific reasoning behind each proposed analogy. Its mission-control-inspired visual design makes the platform engaging while maintaining an emphasis on scientific accuracy.

An important feature is its evidence classification system, which distinguishes satellite-derived estimates, spectral observations, published literature, visual interpretations, and preliminary hypotheses. This helps users understand the reliability and limitations of different scientific findings.

Benefits and intended impact

Mars Analog Explorer aims to demonstrate how studying extreme environments on Earth can contribute to future space exploration. Terrestrial analogs can support astrobiological investigations, geological interpretation, instrument testing, and research relevant to robotic exploration.

The platform also has an educational purpose: making planetary science and satellite data more accessible to students and people interested in space exploration.

Factors considered and limitations

During the investigation, I considered environmental conditions, geological processes, mineral composition, satellite observations, scientific relevance, and the strength of the available evidence.

A central consideration was avoiding unsupported conclusions. Terrestrial environments cannot fully reproduce Martian conditions because of differences in atmospheric pressure, gravity, temperature, and other environmental factors. Additionally, some satellite measurements contain uncertainty, and regional geological findings do not necessarily represent the exact coordinates selected.

For this reason, the project uses qualitative comparisons rather than numerical similarity scores and explicitly identifies limitations and areas requiring further investigation.

Ultimately, Mars Analog Explorer demonstrates that Earth is not only our home planet but also a valuable scientific laboratory for understanding and preparing to explore Mars.
